extraction.name: PIQA
extraction.description: Physical Interaction: Question Answering (PIQA) is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense understanding. The task is multiple choice question answering: given a question and two possible solutions, a model or a human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk; Rowan Zellers; Ronan Le Bras; Jianfeng Gao; Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Yonatan; Zellers, Rowan; Le Bras, Ronan; Gao, Jianfeng; Choi, Yejin. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. 2020.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected as goal-solution pairs for a multiple choice question answering task. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com and asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and use it as inspiration to construct two component tasks. They articulated a physical goal, wrote a valid solution, and provided a permutation of their own solution that makes it invalid, often subtly. Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Additional qualification HITs were run prior to the main collection stage and validation was performed afterwards by other annotators for correctness.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Prompts were derived from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing tasks such as cooking, car repair, crafting, baking, and manipulating objects using everyday materials. Annotators used these instructables as inspiration for creating goal and solution pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm. AFLite discarded instances whose feature representations were highly indicative of the target label. In practice, 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large for the task and compute embeddings of all remaining instances, and an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data was used to identify and remove biased or trivial examples. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples with low agreement were removed during validation. This often removed correct examples that required expert-level domain knowledge. The dataset was further cleaned with AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. Goals were tokenized by Spacy for reporting statistics, and examples were collected in English.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to provide 1) a physical goal, 2) a valid solution, and 3) a trick that should sound reasonable but be wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. Annotators were prompted with instructables to encourage creative, less prototypical uses of everyday objects. A qualification HIT containing well-constructed and underspecified goal-solution pairs was used before participation in the main HIT, and annotators had to identify which were well formed with greater than 80% accuracy to participate. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Human performance was calculated by majority vote, and annotators for human evaluation were chosen from those who achieved at least 90% on the qualification HIT.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. The paper also notes that some development errors on manual inspection were actually correct but required a web search to verify.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors position PIQA as a benchmark to advance language representations that capture physical knowledge useful beyond the NLP community, including for robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. They argue that learning about the world from language alone is limiting and that knowledge should eventually be learned from interaction with the world and communicated with language.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly discusses reporting bias as a challenge in physical commonsense data collection, noting that facts about physical commonsense are rarely directly reported in text. In early unconstrained prompts, reporting bias swamped the dataset because annotators were drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools such as forks, knives, hammers, and drills, and rarely considered other everyday objects. The dataset was also cleaned of annotation artifacts and spurious biases using AFLite.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that text is inherently limited for physical domains due to reporting bias. Some examples removed during validation required expert-level knowledge and were considered outside commonsense. Manual inspection showed that some model 'mistakes' were actually correct but required a web search to verify. The authors also state that learning about the world from language alone is limiting, and that future systems might match humans on the dataset by finding large in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, but that this is not the intended point of the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is introduced as a benchmark for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. It is used for training, development, and testing multiple choice question answering systems, with over 16,000 training pairs and held-out development and test sets. The authors use it to benchmark pretrained language models and as a diagnostic tool to probe models' physical commonsense knowledge.
